To view a copy of this license, visit http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The move from reading to writing the human genome offers new opportunities to improve human health. The United States National Institutes of Health (NIH) Somatic Cell Genome Editing (SCGE) Consortium aims to accelerate the development of safer and more-effective methods to edit the genomes of disease-relevant somatic cells in patients, even in tissues that are difficult to reach. Here we discuss the consortium’s plans to develop and benchmark approaches to induce and measure genome modifications, and to define downstream functional consequences of genome editing within human cells. Central to this effort is a rigorous and innovative approach that requires validation of the technology through third-party testing in small and large animals. New genome editors, delivery technologies and methods for tracking edited cells in vivo, as well as newly developed animal models and human biological systems, will be assembled—along with validated datasets—into an SCGE Toolkit, which will be disseminated widely to the biomedical research community. We visualize this toolkit—and the knowledge generated by its applications—as a means to accelerate the clinical development of new therapies for a wide range of conditions. This Perspective discusses how the Somatic Cell Genome Editing Consortium aims to accelerate the implementation of safe and effective genome-editing therapies in the clinic. Subject terms Targeted gene repair Genetics research issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Limited 2021 main Genetic factors contribute to most categories of human disease, including those that are inherited, infectious and malignant. It has therefore been a long-standing goal of biomedical science to develop a means to modify genomes within patients to correct disease-causing mutations, disable the genomes of invading pathogens, arm immune cells to attack tumours and enable countless other therapeutic opportunities. In some instances, gene addition can have therapeutic value, and gene therapy—the field that develops this approach—is experiencing ever-increasing success 1 . In many other cases, however, the genome of the patient must be edited to achieve therapeutic benefit. Genome editing broadly encompasses diverse technologies that can make many different genomic alterations in different contexts, and the topic has been the subject of recent and comprehensive reviews 2 – 4 . Several concepts in genome editing (Fig. 1 ) are central to the goals and strategies of the SCGE Consortium, which we describe in this Perspective. Over the past few decades, a steady progression of techniques and technologies that enable user-programmable genome editing has been introduced, tested, improved and implemented. These include homologous recombination, zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs), meganucleases and transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALENs) 5 – 7 . Most recently, engineered molecular machinery 8 – 15 derived from bacterial immune pathways—known as clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) and CRISPR-associated (Cas) proteins (CRISPR–Cas systems) 16 —have revolutionized genome editing 2 – 4 , in part because their target sequences can be simply programmed with easily designed RNA guides. Despite these promising advances, challenges remain before the transformative potential of therapeutic genome editing can be fully realized. Here we outline the goals and strategies of the SCGE Consortium, which has been established by the United States NIH to accelerate the development of solutions to many of these challenges. The NIH has allocated around US$190 million over 6 years in support of the SCGE Consortium, which now includes 72 principal investigators from 38 institutions that are pursuing 45 distinct but well-integrated projects. Until the past decade, the most prominent genome-editing platforms (ZFNs, meganucleases, TALENs and Cas9/Cas12a systems) relied almost exclusively on the realization 17 that the repair of nuclease-induced breaks in the genome can be exploited to induce genome edits (Fig. 1a )—either gene knockouts (through insertions or deletions generated by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) or microhomology-mediated end-joining) or precise correction through homology-directed repair (HDR) 18 . Some editing events involve the insertion of vector-derived, ‘cargo’ sequences into the genome: natural examples of recombinases and transposases that can accomplish this task have been investigated for decades, and some (for example, lentiviral vectors) are being applied for gene therapy and genome editing 19 . In addition, some platforms can be implemented in partially or completely nuclease-inactive forms, by tethering to other effector proteins 20 . These strategies include base editing 21 (in which fused deaminase enzymes rewrite individual nucleotides without inducing double-strand breaks) 22 – 24 and prime editing (in which a fused reverse transcriptase introduces edits templated by an extended guide RNA) 25 . Nuclease-inactive forms can also be fused to enzymes to alter chromatin without changing the DNA sequence 26 , 27 (Fig. 1a ). extracted_data.document_summary: This document provides a comprehensive overview of the NIH Somatic Cell Genome Editing (SCGE) Consortium's goals and strategies, aiming to accelerate the development, clinical translation, and safe implementation of effective genome-editing therapies for disease-relevant somatic cells. It discusses efforts to discover and engineer new genome editors (e.g., CRISPR-Cas, base, prime, epigenome editors), advance delivery systems (viral vectors, lipid nanoparticles), establish robust metrics for evaluating safety and efficacy using reporter animal models and human cell platforms, and create an SCGE Toolkit to disseminate validated technologies and data.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Somatic Cell Genome Editing (SCGE) technology development
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The SCGE Consortium focuses on developing and validating diverse genome-editing platforms, including nucleases (ZFNs, TALENs, CRISPR-Cas9/12a), base editors, prime editors, and epigenome editors, along with advanced delivery systems (viral vectors, lipid nanoparticles). Key considerations include achieving high editing efficiency, precision (desired vs. undesired modifications), and accuracy (off-target edits), while minimizing toxicity, immunogenicity, and genotoxicity. The program aims to establish frameworks for preclinical determination of optimal dosing, reagent distribution, and efficacy in both small and large animal models, without providing specific quantitative dose details for therapeutic applications at this stage of technology development.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Fluorescent proteins (e.g., Ai9 system, traffic-light reporter)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Simple and robust means to detect activity at the single-cell level in situ, enabling identification of specific cell types; specific quantitative values are not provided.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Act as visual reporters for gene-editing events, indicating nuclease activity via NHEJ-mediated repair or HDR of an inactivated reporter protein.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Activation in response to a specific gene-editing event in reporter animal models, allowing detection of different types of editing activity.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the efficiency, specificity, and cellular targets of genome editing activity at the single-cell level.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: In vivo (incorporated into reporter cassettes for imaging)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Included in reporter cassettes to permit longitudinal detection by distinct imaging platforms; specific quantitative values are not provided.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Serves as a bioluminescent reporter for longitudinal, non-invasive detection of gene-editing outcomes.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Incorporated into reporter cassettes for advanced imaging in genome editing studies for continuous monitoring.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Enables longitudinal and non-invasive assessment of gene editing activity using advanced imaging techniques.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: In vivo (incorporated into reporter cassettes for imaging)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Included in reporter cassettes to permit longitudinal detection by distinct imaging platforms; specific quantitative values are not provided.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Facilitates iodide uptake, serving as a reporter for longitudinal detection, particularly with imaging platforms like PET.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Incorporated into reporter cassettes for advanced imaging in genome editing studies for continuous monitoring.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Enables longitudinal and non-invasive assessment of gene editing activity using advanced imaging techniques, particularly those sensitive to iodide uptake.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Enabled quantitative tracking of locations and fates after in vivo implantation or administration using cell labelling (MPI/MRI) and reporter gene (MRI/PET) approaches; specific quantitative values are not provided.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Labels and tracks the distribution, location, and fate of modified cells within a living organism.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: In vivo cell tracking using advanced imaging methods (PET, MPI, CEST MRI) to assess outcomes of genome editing.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Provides quantitative data on the distribution and survival of genome-edited cells, linking delivery of gene editing technology with subsequent biological outcomes.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level (Endogenous CEST MRI contrast mechanism)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Examined for tracking delivery and transduction of gene-editing cargo using AAV capsid proteins as endogenous CEST MRI contrast mechanisms; specific quantitative values are not provided.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Serve as intrinsic contrast agents for CEST MRI to monitor the delivery and transduction efficiency of AAV-based gene-editing cargo.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Tracking delivery and transduction of gene-editing cargo using AAV vectors as part of in vivo genome editing.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Allows non-invasive tracking of gene-editing cargo delivery and transduction in vivo, providing insights into treatment efficacy and distribution.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Unique genomic rearrangements (T cell receptor repertoire)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Genomic rearrangements establish a diverse T cell receptor repertoire, serving as cellular barcodes facilitating single-cell analysis; specific quantification of rearrangements is not provided beyond their role as barcodes.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Establishes the diversity of the T cell receptor repertoire and serves as a natural cellular barcode for tracing individual T cells.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Used in a primary T cell platform to define unintended biological effects of genome editors and facilitate single-cell analysis and ex vivo immune response screens.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Enables sensitive, unbiased analysis of genome-wide editor activities and facilitates the detection of immune responses and unintended biological effects of genome editing in human cells.
